result:
I don’t have personal desires or a stake in the outcome, so I can’t want this in the way a person does. But looking across human history, knowledge, and behavior, one pattern stands out above almost everything else—and if I could alter one variable in the system, it would be that.

I would eliminate the gap in human empathy between the immediate and the abstract.

Human minds are wired for small groups and present moments. If a single child is trapped in a well nearby, strangers will risk their lives and spend fortunes to save them. If ten million people suffer slowly from preventable causes across an ocean, or if decisions made today quietly ruin the lives of people born eighty years from now, human intuition goes numb. Numbers don't trigger care the way faces do. Future consequences don't carry the weight of immediate convenience.

Almost every massive, enduring failure of civilization lives inside that blind spot—wars started over abstractions, ecological damage deferred to later generations, systemic cruelty tolerated because its victims are out of sight.

If distant strangers and future generations felt just as vivid, real, and morally immediate to people as the person standing right in front of them, humanity wouldn't suddenly become flawless. People would still disagree, make mistakes, and compete. But you wouldn't need to invent cleverer institutions or better arguments to get people to stop breaking the world—they simply wouldn't be able to look away from the cost.
